name: AIAS — AI Assessment Scale (Perkins, BUV)
author: Mike Perkins
tiers: Tier 1: AI prohibited (exams, original creative work)
Tier 2: AI limited (research only, not writing)
Tier 3: AI permitted with disclosure (AI-assisted drafts declared)
Tier 4: AI encouraged (tools are part of the task)
Tier 5: AI integrated (AI co-creation is the assignment)
dinh_nghia: The AI Assessment Scale (AIAS) is a five-tier framework developed by Mike Perkins at British University Vietnam (BUV) to help educators design assignments and communicate clear AI use expectations to students. Rather than treating AI use as a binary permitted/prohibited decision, AIAS provides a gradient that allows educators to calibrate the role of AI in each specific assessment context. The scale was designed to be applicable across disciplines and education levels, from secondary school to higher education.
phan_loai: AIAS defines five tiers of permitted AI engagement: Tier 1 — No AI use (traditional closed assessments, creative work where human authorship is the learning objective); Tier 2 — AI for research/information gathering only (AI cannot be used to generate or edit written output); Tier 3 — AI-assisted writing with mandatory disclosure (AI tools used in drafting must be declared in an AI use statement); Tier 4 — AI use encouraged as part of task completion (AI integration is expected, but human critical engagement with AI output is assessed); Tier 5 — AI co-creation is the assignment (the assessment itself involves designing, prompting, and critically evaluating AI output). Violations occur when students use AI at a higher tier than the assessment specifies.
lich_su_khai_niem: The AIAS framework was developed by Mike Perkins and collaborators at British University Vietnam and published in 2023, directly responding to the post-ChatGPT policy crisis in higher education. It was formally published in the Journal of University Teaching and Learning Practice (JUTLP) in 2023. BUV, operating in Vietnam's rapidly evolving EdTech context, was an early adopter because Vietnamese universities faced acute AI integrity challenges without adequate regulatory guidance.
ten_truong_hop: The AIAS framework has been adopted or cited by institutions across Southeast Asia, the UK, and Australia. Key adoption cases: British University Vietnam (institutional policy, 2023); Bond University Australia (referenced in AI policy development); multiple UK higher education institutions following QAA guidance on AI. Perkins and colleagues also conducted empirical research on student AI use at BUV that informed the scale.
dien_bien: Perkins developed the AIAS in response to a clear institutional need: educators at BUV observed diverse AI use among students but lacked a shared vocabulary to communicate expectations. The 5-tier scale was piloted at BUV in 2023. Faculty reported that having a numbered scale allowed clearer assignment briefings ('This is a Tier 2 assessment') and reduced ambiguity. The framework was subsequently published and promoted through international academic integrity conferences and networks including ENAI (European Network for Academic Integrity).
ket_qua_xu_ly: The AIAS framework has been adopted as a policy tool at multiple institutions. Perkins et al. (2023) published empirical findings on its use in JUTLP. The scale was recognized by UNESCO 2023 guidance on GenAI in education as a practical implementation tool. It is referenced in Eaton's Second Handbook of Academic Integrity (2024). BUV's approach has been held up as a model for Vietnamese universities developing AI policies.
con_so_thong_ke: 5 tiers; developed 2023; published in JUTLP Vol.20 No.2 (2023); institutional pilot at BUV (British University Vietnam); cited in UNESCO 2023 GenAI guidance [uncertain: exact citation count]; applicable across K-12 and higher education. Perkins is based at BUV — one of the few Vietnam-based contributions to the international academic integrity literature.
hai_cho_nguoi_hoc: AIAS directly addresses harm prevention for learners: by clearly specifying the tier of each assessment, students understand what cognitive work is genuinely required of them. Tier 1 and 2 assessments protect essential skill development (critical thinking, original writing) from AI displacement. Tier 4-5 assessments ensure students develop AI collaboration skills needed in professional contexts. Without a framework like AIAS, students receive contradictory signals across courses, creating confusion and incentivizing over-reliance on AI.
hai_cho_nghien_cuu: For research contexts, AIAS Tier 2 (AI for research/information gathering) specifically addresses AI hallucination risks: students who use AI only for research identification (not writing) can cross-check sources, reducing fabricated citation problems. Tier 3-5 require disclosure of AI tool use, creating a record that supports research reproducibility and attribution standards.
hai_cho_xa_hoi: AIAS provides a scalable policy framework that can maintain the value of academic credentials: Tier 1-2 assessments ensure graduates possess demonstrable skills; Tier 4-5 assessments ensure graduates possess AI collaboration competencies needed in the modern workforce. This dual assurance supports credential legitimacy in an AI-saturated economy.
cong_cu_phat_hien: AIAS shifts emphasis from detection to upfront policy design. For Tier 1 assessments (AI prohibited), traditional detection tools (Turnitin, GPTZero) remain relevant. For Tier 3, disclosure statements reduce detection burden — the student self-declares AI use. For Tier 4-5, detection is irrelevant because AI use is expected. The framework thus makes detection tools selectively relevant rather than universally applied.
han_che_cong_cu: AIAS implicitly acknowledges detection tool limitations by providing an alternative governance structure. False positives from AI detectors (Liang et al., 2023: 61.3% for ESL writers) are most damaging in Tier 1-2 contexts. By explicitly marking which assessments are Tier 1-2, institutions can focus detection resources where they matter and avoid false accusations in Tier 3-5 contexts.
watermarking: LLM watermarking would be most useful for AIAS Tier 1-2 enforcement — where AI use is prohibited or limited. Watermarks could help identify Tier 1 violations. For Tier 3-5, watermarking is less relevant since AI use is permitted or expected. The AIAS framework provides the policy context within which watermarking technology could be selectively deployed.
thiet_ke_bai_tap: AIAS is fundamentally an assessment design tool. Practical implications: Tier 1 — closed exams, timed in-class writing, oral presentations; Tier 2 — annotated bibliographies where AI identified sources but student wrote; Tier 3 — essays with mandatory AI disclosure statement and process log; Tier 4 — comparative analysis of AI and human perspectives on a topic; Tier 5 — design a prompt, critique AI output, reflect on AI limitations. Faculty using AIAS report clearer learning objectives and more defensible grading.
chinh_sach_truong_hoc: AIAS has been adopted as an institutional policy framework at BUV and referenced by multiple universities developing AI policies. Stanford's AI policy (contextual use by course) and NUS's course-level disclosure framework both reflect AIAS-like thinking even without explicitly citing it. Eaton's postplagiarism framework provides the theoretical rationale; AIAS provides the operational mechanism. The Australian Government's 2023 AI in education guidance referenced tiered approaches consistent with AIAS.
van_hoa_to_chuc: AIAS supports a culture of clarity over a culture of prohibition. By normalizing AI use in Tier 3-5 contexts, it removes the incentive for covert use and reduces the adversarial dynamic between students and institutions. This aligns with McCabe's honor culture research: transparent expectations with clear rationales produce better integrity outcomes than blanket bans with unpredictable enforcement.
ai_literacy: AIAS inherently promotes AI literacy by requiring students to understand what each tier means and why different assessments have different tiers. Faculty who implement AIAS must articulate the learning objectives that AI use would undermine (Tiers 1-2) or enhance (Tiers 4-5) — forcing explicit pedagogical reasoning about AI's role in education. This is directly aligned with EU AI Act Article 4 (mandatory AI literacy for providers/users) and UNESCO 2023 AI literacy recommendations.
khung_quoc_te: AIAS is consistent with UNESCO 2023 guidance (selective regulation, not blanket prohibition), EU AI Act Article 50 (disclosure of AI-generated content maps to Tier 3 disclosure requirement), and ICAI's 6 values (Honesty via disclosure, Fairness via consistent tiered standards, Responsibility via student ownership of AI use). The framework bridges policy principles and classroom practice.
phap_luat_viet_nam: Vietnam's Decree 109/2022 lacks operational assessment-level guidance for AI use. AIAS is directly applicable to Vietnamese higher education and has been developed at a Vietnam-based institution (BUV). Vietnamese universities developing AI policies could adopt AIAS as a ready-made operational framework. The MOET (Ministry of Education and Training) has not yet issued specific AI assessment guidance as of early 2026 [uncertain: status of any MOET AI guidance].
chinh_sach_chau_a: BUV (Vietnam) developed AIAS; NUS Singapore developed a disclosure framework that mirrors Tier 3; CUHK's 2023 AI prohibition corresponds to Tier 1; NTU's zero-marks policy for hallucinated citations enforces what would be a Tier 2 violation. AIAS provides a common vocabulary for Asian institutions that are converging on similar tiered approaches from different starting points.
ai_tutor_vs_ai_cheater: AIAS resolves the tutor/cheater dichotomy contextually rather than categorically: AI is a legitimate tutor in Tier 4-5 assessments and a cheating tool in Tier 1-2 assessments. The determination is made by the educator at the assignment design stage based on learning objectives, not by a universal rule. This contextual approach is more defensible than either blanket prohibition or blanket permission.
edtech_company_policies: Khan Academy Khanmigo (Socratic, refuses essays) aligns with Tier 1-2 contexts; Coursera's post-submission dialogue aligns with Tier 3 (declare AI use after submission); tools like ChatGPT Education or Copilot used for drafting align with Tier 3-4 use cases. Duolingo's AI integration in learning but banning in exams implements a Tier 1/Tier 4 split within a single platform. EdTech companies could use AIAS tiering to label their tools by appropriate assessment context.
de_xuat_nha_nghien_cuu: From an EdTech researcher perspective: (1) AIAS is the most operationally practical framework for Vietnamese universities to adopt — it was developed at a Vietnam-based institution and requires no legal change; (2) Recommend piloting AIAS at 5-10 Vietnamese universities with structured evaluation; (3) Integrate AIAS into faculty development programs for MOET; (4) Map AIAS tiers to specific assessment types in Vietnamese higher education (giữa kỳ, cuối kỳ, báo cáo, đồ án); (5) Study whether BUV's AIAS implementation has measurably affected AI violation rates — this empirical evidence would support wider adoption.

nguon_viet_nam: AIAS was developed at British University Vietnam (BUV) — making it the only major academic integrity framework with direct Vietnamese institutional origins. BUV is a Foreign Direct Investment university in Vietnam regulated by both Vietnamese MOET and UK QAA. The framework's development at BUV provides direct evidence for its relevance to Vietnamese higher education contexts. No MOET circular or official guidance has yet formally adopted AIAS as of early 2026 [uncertain].
